formal.anchor: Gita layer: Kṣetrajña | Kṣetra (Knower ↔ Field). Linga-Yoni interpretive layer: Active Principle | Transformative Field (Linga ↔ Yoni). KnowledgeOS layer: Initiation → Interaction → Discrimination → Assessment → Transformation. This gives us three different levels, rather than pretending they are identical.

governance.anchor: I think the Gita model may actually be a better home for the Linga-Yoni idea than KnowledgeOS itself. KnowledgeOS can then borrow the structural insight without adopting the metaphysics: Gita: philosophical model → Linga-Yoni: interpretive lens → KnowledgeOS: abstract structural hypothesis. That direction respects the provenance discipline we've established.

lexical.anchor: Kṣetra ≠ Kṣetrajña. A field contains changing phenomena, conditions and processes, while the knower is not simply identical with those changing contents. ... Yoni ≈ Field of manifestation/transformation rather than: Yoni = Knowledge.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The Gita has a third element that prevents us from reducing everything to Linga-Yoni: Kṣetrajña the knower. ... We may need: Knower + Active Principle + Field ... 𝒥 | 𝒜 | ℱ where 𝒥=Knower/knowing standpoint, 𝒜=active/projective principle, ℱ=field of manifestation/transformation.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues a simple Linga x Yoni model is insufficient for the Gita because it omits Ksetrajna (the knower), proposing instead a three-part model Knower(J) | ActivePrinciple(A) | Field(F) as potentially more interesting than importing a two-pole Linga-Yoni into KnowledgeOS.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Generation + Examination ⇏ Progress. For a Gita model, this is actually quite natural. The Gita does not say that merely producing more mental activity constitutes knowledge. There is a crucial role for: Viveka -- discrimination/discernment. So perhaps the Gita model gives us the missing third operation: Generation → Field interaction → Discrimination → Transformation.
rationale_evidence.statement: Connects the S2453/S2457 empirical finding (Generation+Examination does not imply Progress) to the Gita's concept of Viveka (discrimination/discernment) as a candidate missing third operation: Generation -> Field interaction -> Discrimination -> Transformation, rather than the tested-and-failed Generation -> Examination -> Knowledge pipeline.
